{{short description|American mathematicians}}

'''David Volfovich Chudnovsky'''{{efn|{{langx|uk|Давид Вольфович Чудновський|{{transliteration|uk|ukrainian|Davyd Volfovych Chudnovskyi}}}}, {{lang|ru|Давид Вольфович Чудновский}}}} (born January 22, 1947) and '''Gregory Volfovich Chudnovsky'''{{efn|{{langx|uk|Григорій Вольфович Чудновський|{{transliteration|uk|ukrainian|Hryhorii Volfovych Chudnovskyi}}}}, {{lang|ru|Григорий Вольфович Чудновский}}}} (born April 17, 1952) are American [[mathematician]]s and engineers known for their world-record mathematical calculations and developing the [[Chudnovsky algorithm]] used to calculate the digits of [[pi|{{pi}}]] with extreme precision. Both were born in [[Kiev]], [[Ukrainian SSR]], [[Soviet Union]] (now [[Kyiv]], [[Ukraine]]).

==Careers in mathematics==
As a child, Gregory Chudnovsky was given a copy of ''[[What Is Mathematics?]]'' by his father (Volf Grigorovich Chudnovski, a Soviet professor of technical sciences)  and decided that he wanted to be a mathematician. As a high schooler, he solved [[Hilbert's tenth problem]], shortly after [[Yuri Matiyasevich]] had solved it.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chudnovsky's contribution to MRDP|author=Martin Davis|accessdate=27 November 2022|publisher=FOM mailing list|date=February 10, 1998|url=https://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/1998-February/001172.html}}</ref> He received a mathematics degree from [[Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv|Kyiv State University]] in 1974 and a [[PhD]] the following year from the [[NASU Institute of Mathematics|Institute of Mathematics]], [[National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine]].<ref name="macarthur" />

In part to avoid [[History of the Jews in Ukraine|religious persecution]] and in part to seek better medical care for Gregory, who had been diagnosed with [[myasthenia gravis]], a [[neuromuscular disease]], the Chudnovsky family applied in 1976 for permission to emigrate from the [[Soviet Union]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kiernan |first1=Vincent |title=With Abstruse Mathematics as a Tool, 2 Brothers Tackle Real-World Problems |url=https://www.chronicle.com/article/with-abstruse-mathematics-as-a-tool-2-brothers-tackle-real-world-problems/ |accessdate=19 October 2020 |work=[[The Chronicle of Higher Education]] |date=March 20, 1998}}</ref><ref name="macarthur">{{cite web |title=Gregory V. Chudnovsky - MacArthur Foundation |url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/75/ |website=www.macfound.org |publisher=[[MacArthur Foundation]] |accessdate=19 October 2020}}</ref> Although the family was harassed by the [[KGB]] for attempting to leave the country, the brothers were eventually able to secure their emigration with the help of [[United States Senator]] [[Henry M. Jackson]] and mathematician [[Edwin Hewitt]].<ref name="preston">{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=Richard |title=Panic in Level 4: Cannibals, Killer Viruses, and Other Journeys to the Edge of Science |date=2008 |publisher=Random House Publishing Group |isbn=978-1-58836-728-0 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hrdqCFEeFJYC |accessdate=19 October 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

A 1992 article in ''[[The New Yorker]]'' quoted the opinion of several mathematicians that Gregory Chudnovsky was one of the world's best living mathematicians. David Chudnovsky works closely with and assists his brother Gregory.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1992/03/02/the-mountains-of-pi |title=The Mountains of Pi |magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |first=Richard |last=Preston |date=March 1, 1992}}</ref>

Despite their accomplishments and the attention brought to them by their profile in ''The New Yorker'', the Chudnovsky brothers largely worked alone for decades. A 1997 [[Karen Arenson]] article in ''[[The New York Times]]'' theorized that this was due to some combination of the brothers' lack of a specialization (they worked on topics including [[number theory]], [[applied physics]] and [[computer science|computers]]), Gregory's medical condition, their refusal to leave [[New York City]] and their insistence on being hired together. In the summer of 1997, they were hired as professors at [[New York University Tandon School of Engineering|Polytechnic University]] in [[Brooklyn]] after [[borough president]] [[Howard Golden]] helped find funding for their salaries.<ref name="arenson">{{cite news |last1=Arenson |first1=Karen W. |title=For Brilliant Brothers, Joining Mathematics Faculty Is a Quantum Leap |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/12/24/nyregion/for-brilliant-brothers-joining-mathematics-faculty-is-a-quantum-leap.html |accessdate=19 October 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=24 December 1997}}</ref>

The Chudnovsky brothers have held records, at different times, for computing [[pi|{{pi}}]] to the largest number of places, including two billion digits in the early 1990s on a supercomputer they built (dubbed "m-zero") in their apartment in [[Manhattan]]. In 1987, the Chudnovsky brothers developed the algorithm (now called the [[Chudnovsky algorithm]]) that they used to break several {{pi}} computation records. Today, this algorithm is used by [[Mathematica]] to calculate {{pi}}, and has continued to be used by others who have achieved [[world record]]s [[Chronology of computation of π|in pi calculation]].

The brothers also assisted the [[Metropolitan Museum of Art]] around 2003 in the merging of a series of digital photographs taken of ''[[The Hunt of the Unicorn]]'' tapestries during their cleaning.<ref name="NOW">{{cite web
  | title = NOVA Science NOW
  | publisher = PBS
  | date = 2005-07-26
  | url =https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/video/profile-brothers-chudnovsky/}}</ref> [[Public Broadcasting Service|PBS]] aired a program on its science show ''[[Nova (American TV series)|Nova]]'', hosted by [[Robert Krulwich]], that described the difficulties in photographing the tapestries and the math used to fix them.<ref>
{{cite magazine | first = Richard |last = Preston |authorlink=Richard Preston| title = Capturing the Unicorn | url = http://www.newyorker.com/archive/2005/04/11/050411fa_fact | magazine = The New Yorker | date = 2005-04-11 }}
</ref>

The brothers later became Distinguished Industry Professors at the [[New York University Tandon School of Engineering]], where they work on subjects such as [[graph isomorphism]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://engineering.nyu.edu/our-engineers/faculty/chudnovsky-brothers | title=The Chudnovsky Brothers &#124; NYU Tandon School of Engineering }}</ref> Gregory was awarded the [[MacArthur Fellowship]] (also known as the "Genius Grant") in 1981.
